title: Super Stardust Delta
subtitle: A planet becomes a shooting arena
summary: Super Stardust Delta is Housemarque's PlayStation Vita arcade shooter, first released in Japan on 19 January 2012. The player guides a small ship around a planet while asteroids and enemies occupy the surrounding orbit. The Vita's two analogue sticks separate movement from firing, allowing the ship to escape in one direction while clearing another. A curved playfield keeps the action contained without making it flat. The player is continually looking for a safer route through a space that is being filled and broken apart by incoming objects and weapon fire.
body: Super Stardust Delta is Housemarque's PlayStation Vita arcade shooter, first released in Japan on 19 January 2012. The player guides a small ship around a planet while asteroids and enemies occupy the surrounding orbit. The Vita's two analogue sticks separate movement from firing, allowing the ship to escape in one direction while clearing another. A curved playfield keeps the action contained without making it flat. The player is continually looking for a safer route through a space that is being filled and broken apart by incoming objects and weapon fire.

Ice and Fire weapons have different strengths against the objects appearing in the field, making quick switching part of an efficient defence. Pickups strengthen the ship, while bombs offer a way to recover when the surrounding space becomes difficult to read. Different bomb effects connect to the Vita's touch and motion inputs, adding another response beyond the two sticks. The player has to recognise when ordinary movement and firing can still solve the situation and when a stronger intervention is needed to reopen a useful path through the debris.

Harri Tikkanen directed the game and Ari Pulkkinen composed its music. The main arcade mode contains five planets divided into phases, each concluding with a boss. North American and PAL releases followed in February 2012 around the handheld's wider launch. Housemarque adapted a familiar series to a machine whose paired sticks could preserve its immediate control while touch surfaces supplied additional effects. The result offers a compact demonstration of the Vita's possibilities without losing the central arcade task: stay alive, remove the next threat and keep enough of the orbit clear to continue moving.
